passages.happening:
God gives Moses a law for anyone, ‘a man or woman’, who ‘makes a special vow, the vow of a Nazirite, to separate himself to the LORD’ (verse 2).

Three things mark the vow. The Nazirite drinks no wine or strong drink and eats nothing from the grapevine, ‘not even the seeds or skins’ (verses 3-4). “For the entire period of his vow of separation, no razor shall pass over his head” (verse 5). And he does not go near a dead body, even if a parent, a brother or a sister should die (verses 6-7).

“Throughout the time of his separation, he is holy to the LORD” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 5 kept the camp from being defiled. Chapter 6 shows the opposite movement. An ordinary Israelite, who is not a priest or a Levite, chooses to come nearer to God for a time.

The word Nazirite is related to the Hebrew nezer, which means separation or consecration. The law does not invent the vow. It assumes such vows were already known and gives them a form.

The vow was open to women as well as men. In a camp where the priesthood belonged to one family and the care of the tent to one tribe, here was a way for anyone to step toward the center.

Each of the three rules borrows a mark of the priests. Priests could not drink wine when they entered the tent (Leviticus 10:9). The high priest could not go near a dead body even for his father or mother (Leviticus 21:11), and the Nazirite is held to that same highest standard. The uncut hair is called ‘the crown of consecration’ (verse 7). The Hebrew word, nezer, is also the word for the holy crown on the high priest's turban (Exodus 29:6). For the length of the vow, a farmer or a woman of the household lived with something like a high priest's holiness.

The rules were visible, and they cost something. Wine and grapes were part of daily life and of every celebration. Long uncut hair told everyone who saw it that a vow had been made. And in a world where families washed and buried their own dead, a Nazirite could not do the last duties of love for a parent.

Nothing in the law treats wine, haircuts or funerals as bad. The Nazirite gave up good things for a time, as a sign of belonging wholly to God.
passages.later:
Samson was to be ‘a Nazirite to God from the womb’ (Judges 13:5), which was unusual, because his vow was for life and was given by God before his birth. Hannah vowed that no razor would touch the head of her son Samuel (1 Samuel 1:11). The prophet Amos accused Israel of spoiling the vows of others: “But you made the Nazirites drink wine” (Amos 2:12).

In the New Testament the angel says of John the Baptist, ‘He shall never take wine or strong drink’ (Luke 1:15). Paul ‘had his head shaved in Cenchrea to keep a vow he had made’ (Acts 18:18), and later paid the costs of four men completing vows at the temple (Acts 21:23-24), which most interpreters take to be Nazirite vows.

Jesus was called a Nazarene because he grew up in Nazareth. He was not a Nazirite. He drank wine (Luke 7:34), and he touched the dead to raise them.
passages.asks: An ordinary person could choose, for a time, to belong to God in a way everyone could see. Ask whether there is some good thing you could set aside for a season in order to give your attention to God. And ask whether your faith costs you anything that another person could notice.

passages.t: A vow broken, and a vow completed
passages.happening:
Sometimes a vow was broken through no fault of the Nazirite. “If someone suddenly dies in his presence and defiles his consecrated head of hair, he must shave his head on the day of his cleansing” (verse 9). He brings two birds to the priest, and then begins the whole vow again. “But the preceding days shall not be counted, because his separation was defiled” (verse 12).

When the time of the vow is complete, the Nazirite comes to the entrance of the tent with a burnt offering, a sin offering and a peace offering, with bread, grain and drink offerings (verses 13-17). He shaves his head and puts the hair ‘on the fire under the peace offering’ (verse 18). The priest waves a share of the offering before the LORD. “After that, the Nazirite may drink wine” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
The law is realistic. People die without warning, and a Nazirite might be standing beside them. The law does not blame him. It gives him a way to begin again.

Starting over was costly. All the days already kept were lost. That shows how seriously God took a promise freely made. It also shows mercy. The vow was not ruined for good. It could be taken up again from the first day.

The ceremony at the end was a celebration. The peace offering was the one sacrifice the worshiper ate, a meal shared before God. The hair, the sign of the vow, was burned in its fire. Then the Nazirite drank wine again and went back to ordinary life. The vow had an end as well as a beginning, and returning to common things was no failure.

Verse 21 adds that the Nazirite brings these offerings ‘in addition to whatever else he can afford’. The vow came with a real cost, and each person gave beyond it as they were able.
passages.later:
Ecclesiastes warns about the weight of a promise made to God: “It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it” (Ecclesiastes 5:5).

The four men whose expenses Paul paid were completing vows in the way this passage describes, ‘so they can have their heads shaved’ (Acts 21:24).
passages.hard:
Why does the Nazirite need a sin offering when someone dies suddenly beside him? How can that be a sin?

Verse 11 says he ‘has sinned by being in the presence of the dead body’, though he could not have prevented it.

Readers explain this in two ways. The scholar Jacob Milgrom argued that the offering traditionally called the sin offering is better called a purification offering. Its purpose is to cleanse the sanctuary and the person from defilement, not to punish guilt. The Hebrew verb behind ‘sin’ can mean to miss a mark. On this reading the Nazirite has done nothing morally wrong. His vow has been interrupted, and the interruption has to be dealt with.

Others keep the traditional name and point out that the Old Testament knows of unintended sins that still need atonement.

On either reading the passage is not teaching that a person is to blame for a death he happened to witness. Anyone who was present when someone died, and has carried guilt for it since, should not hear this verse as an accusation.
passages.asks: A broken vow could be begun again from the first day. Ask what promise to God you made and let fall, and whether you have assumed it could never be taken up again. And ask what it would mean to start it over today.

passages.t: The LORD bless you and keep you
passages.happening:
God gives Aaron and his sons the words they are to speak over Israel.

“‘May the LORD bless you and keep you; may the LORD cause His face to shine upon you and be gracious to you; may the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace’” (verses 24-26).

Then God says what the words do. “So they shall put My name on the Israelites, and I will bless them” (verse 27).
passages.hearers:
After all the counting, arranging and guarding of these chapters, the laws given at Sinai close with a gift. These are among the best-loved words in the Bible, and they deserve to be read slowly.

In Hebrew the blessing is a small poem of three lines, and the lines grow: three words, then five, then seven. Each line names the LORD once, so that God's name is spoken three times over the people.

Each line has two verbs, and the second opens up the first.

To bless is to keep. In Hebrew thought, to bless is to give life, fruitfulness and well-being. To keep is to guard. The people about to enter a wilderness are placed under God's protection.

For God's face to shine is for him to be gracious. A face that shines is a face that is glad to see you. The picture is of a king who turns toward someone who has come with a request, and smiles. To be gracious is to give what has not been earned.

For God to lift up his face is to give peace. The opposite, God hiding his face, is the Bible's picture of being abandoned. Here God looks straight at his people. And the last word of the blessing is its goal: shalom. It means more than the absence of conflict. It is wholeness, safety, health, and things made right with God and with other people.

Then comes verse 27, which guards against a misunderstanding. The priests speak, but they do not bless by any power of their own. God says, ‘I will bless them.’ The words put his name on the people. The blessing is his to give, and he has told the priests to say it so that Israel will know he means to give it.

This blessing is among the oldest pieces of the Bible ever found. In 1979 two tiny silver scrolls were discovered at Ketef Hinnom in Jerusalem, dated to about 600 BC. They carry a form of these words. They were probably worn as amulets, and they show that the blessing was known and treasured in Jerusalem before the exile to Babylon.
passages.later:
The Psalms pray this blessing back to God: “May God be gracious to us and bless us, and cause His face to shine upon us” (Psalm 67:1).

Paul finds the shining face of God in Jesus. God has given ‘the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ’ (2 Corinthians 4:6). And when Paul begins and ends his letters with grace and peace, he is using the two great words of the blessing's last lines.

Luke's Gospel ends with the risen Jesus doing what Aaron did: “He lifted up His hands and blessed them” (Luke 24:50). Many readers have seen there a priest blessing his people. It is a pattern fulfilled, not a prediction made in this chapter.
passages.asks: God told the priests to say these words so that his people would know he meant to bless them. Read the three lines aloud, slowly, as words spoken to you. Ask which of these gifts you most need now: to be kept, to be looked on with gladness, to be given peace. And ask over whom you could speak this blessing this week.
